messages.body_plain:
Hello, good day to everyone.

--I am using the ectotherm function in NicheMapR with the dynamic energy budget (DEB) parameter enabled to predict activity, morphology, and demographic variables of a tropical sceloporine lizard. My study is framed in various geographical points during three successive months of a particular year (2017).
--I know that I must use micro_global to predict the microclimate used by ecototherm for its calculations, and that I can extract from the predictions the data corresponding to the months and hours of interest.
--However, I need to be able to specify the year in question, not a number of years from the climate database that micro_global handles by default. I can specify the year and months with micro_ncep, but I have not been able to run ectotherm with DEB=1 using micro_ncep. I think I could use micro_terra for that task because it has the nyear parameter, but I'm not sure.

I have two questions, first, which NicheMapR microclimatic function (where I can specify a particular year) can I concatenate with the ectotherm function (with parameter DEB=1) to obtain morphological (mass) and demographic (intrinsic rate of natural increase) variables.
Second, if this cannot be done with micro_terra, is there a tutorial where I can learn how to replace the micro_global climatic database with another corresponding to the year 2017?

Thank you very much in advance for your time and interest.

That was a necessary step because I am interested in calculating the mass and intrinsic rate of natural growth of adult lizards during the hottest quarter (March 1 to May 30) of 2017 at my study site (in Morelos, Mexico; e.g., -99.19706,18.45588). But, although I set the initial stage at the reproductive adult stage (stage <- 3), the ectotherm function starts calculations from the juvenile stage (stage <- 2), which can be seen in the figure to be generated (at the end of the script). I am interested then that the ectotherm begins with the calculations from the adult stage.

* Also, when running the period between 2016-01-02 to 2018-12-30, I expected the mass increase curve to stop at 36g, but instead it kept changing
up to 51.7g. I don't understand why that would happen.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Israel,

When you turn the DEB model on, the Ww_g parameter no longer specifies the weight - it is driven by the DEB model and its parameters (in your case, for Eulamprus quoyii). You started the model at 'puberty'. This is not maximum size but when the lizard is mature which means it's started to allocate to reproduction. So it grows from 12 g to the maximum size of ~50 g. But note that debout$WETMASS is including reproduction buffer (and stomach contents), and the sudden drops were it laying a clutch.  If you want it to start at the maximum size, you need to specify the initial structure as L.m^3 not L.p^3 (i.e., maximum length cubed, not length at puberty cubed).

Re the shade - yes you need to make sure it's a vector of the same number of days as the microclimate output. You can just not specify it in the call to 'ectotherm' if you want to make it the same as what the microclimate model was run at, because by default it takes micro$MINSHADES and micro$MAXSHADES as input. I had no problem running it for the different date ranges. Just try without specifying minshade and maxshade and it should work, then you can debug what's going wrong from there if you're still having trouble specifying shade manually.

Also, note that in the current version the DEB parameter input F.m should now be p.Xm, i.e., replace
F_m=F.m
with
p_Xm = p.Xm
in the call to the ectotherm model.

Note that the ectotherm model expects microclimate input in a particular format, but you can overwrite that with whatever you want and make manually constructed versions e.g. of metout, shadmet etc. You just have to be careful to keep the same number of days/hours for each input variable or else the program will crash due to memory problems.

All the best,
Mike

You started the model at 'puberty'. This is not maximum size but when the lizard is mature which means it's started to allocate to reproduction. So it grows from 12 g to the maximum size of ~50 g. But note that debout$WETMASS is including reproduction buffer (and stomach contents), and the sudden drops were it laying a clutch.  If you want it to start at the maximum size, you need to specify the initial structure as L.m^3 not L.p^3 (i.e., maximum length cubed, not length at puberty cubed).
>
> Re the shade - yes you need to make sure it's a vector of the same number of days as the microclimate output. You can just not specify it in the call to 'ectotherm' if you want to make it the same as what the microclimate model was run at, because by default it takes micro$MINSHADES and micro$MAXSHADES as input. I had no problem running it for the different date ranges. Just try without specifying minshade and maxshade and it should work, then you can debug what's going wrong from there if you're still having trouble specifying shade manually.

messages.body_plain:
Dear NicheMapR users,

I've just finished (and pushed to the github repository) a modularisation of the ectotherm model, function 'ectoR_devel' which is similar in usage and approach to endoR_devel. It doesn't include any behaviour or the Dynamic Energy Budget models etc. of the 'ectotherm' function, just the heat budget. It is fully in R based on R conversions of the relevant Fortran code from 'ectotherm'.

It will be useful for learning and teaching the model, testing its behaviour, and for the development of customised behavoiural routines and integrations with metabolic theory.

Here is the full list of new functions that ectoR_devel uses:

GEOM_ecto (calculates biophyiscally relevant surfaces, volumes and dimensions)
SOLAR_ecto (calculates incoming solar)
RADIN_ecto (calculates incoming long-wave radiation)
RADOUT_ecto (calculates outgoing long-wave radiation)

  alpha = 0.85, # solar absorptivity

plot(time, TC, type = 'l', ylim = c(-25, 55), ylab = 'body temperature, deg C', xlab = 'month of year')
points(time, TC_ectotherm, type = 'l', col = 2)

# run microclimate model in monthly mode at default site (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
micro <- micro_global()

# extract full sun conditions
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)

# get required inputs
TAs <- metout$TALOC
TGRDs <- soil$D0cm
TSKYs <- metout$TSKYC
VELs <- metout$VLOC
RHs <- metout$RHLOC
QSOLRs <- metout$SOLR
Zs <- metout$ZEN

# use ectoR_devel to compute body temperature in open without respiratory heat loss,
# conduction, or metabolic heat gain
TC <- unlist(lapply(1:length(TAs), function(x){ectoR_devel(
  Ww_g = 40, # wet weight, g
  shape = 3, # using lizard geometry
  alpha = 0.85, # solar absorptivity
  M_1 = 0, # turn of metabolic heat
  postur = 0, # average posture, half way between normal and parallel to sun
  pantmax = 0, # turn off respiratory heat exchange

  pct_cond = 40, # negligible conduction to substrate
  K_sub = 0.1,

  alpha_sub = (1 - micro$REF), # substrate absorptivity used in microclimate model
  elev = micro$elev, # elevation from microclimate model
  TA = TAs[x], # air temperature at lizard height from microclimate model, deg C
  TGRD = TGRDs[x], # ground temperature from microclimate model, deg C

  TSUBST = TGRDs[x], # ground temperature from microclimate model, deg C

  TSKY = TSKYs[x], # sky temperature from microclimate model, deg C
  VEL = VELs[x], # wind speed from microclimate model, m/s
  RH = RHs[x], # relative humidity from microclimate model, %
  QSOLR = QSOLRs[x], # total horizontal plane solar radiation from microclimate model, W/m2
  Z = Zs[x] # solar zenith angle from microclimate model, degrees
)$TC})) # run ectoR_devel across environments

# run ectotherm model for a non-behaving animal without respiratory heat loss,
# conduction or metabolic heat gain

micro$tcond[, 3] <- 0.1 # set K_sub (equally, you could make the input for ectoR_devel come from micro$tcond)

ecto <- ectotherm(
  Ww_g = 40, # wet weight, g
  shape = 3, # using lizard geometry
  alpha_min = 0.85, # minimum solar absorptivity
  alpha_max = 0.85, # maximum solar absorptivity
  M_1 = 0, # turn of metabolic heat
  postur = 0, # average posture, half way between normal and parallel to sun
  pantmax = 0, # turn off respiratory heat exchange

  pct_cond = 40, # negligible conduction to substrate

  live = 0
)

# extract results
environ <- as.data.frame(ecto$environ)
enbal <- as.data.frame(ecto$enbal)
masbal <- as.data.frame(ecto$masbal)
TC_ectotherm <- environ$TC

# compare
time <- micro$dates
plot(time, TC, type = 'l', ylim = c(-25, 55), ylab = 'body temperature, deg C', xlab = 'month of year')
points(time, TC_ectotherm, type = 'l', col = 2)

Hi Israel,

For question 1, you are manually counting times that Tb is within certain limits but not checking to see if it is nighttime / dusk and the animal is diurnal - I suspect that's the problem.
For question 2, you have redefined parameters after getting the parameters out of the allstat list. The result is that your specified initial conditions for structure and reserve density are higher than what they should be and the animal heads down towards the steady state. You shouldn't change the parameters from those you get out of allstat.
For question 3, did you see the recent message I sent about ectoR_devel? That has all the code to compute Tb. It finds the heat fluxes for all the different heat exchange mechanisms, (QSOLAR, QIRIN, QMET, QIROUT, QCONV, etc.), and then iteratively guesses the Tb that balances the heat budget. For the DEB theory, wet mass is calculated based on the current values of structure, reserve, reproduction buffer and stomach contents. The code is in the ectotherm Fortran code but also in the R DEB functions in NicheMapR, e.g. the code:
  wetgonad <- ((E_R / mu_E) * w_E) / d_Egg + ((E_B / mu_E) * w_E) / d_Egg
  wetstorage <- ((V * E / mu_E) * w_E) / d_E
  wetgut <- ((E_s / mu_E) * w_E) / fdry
  wetmass <- V * andens_deb + wetgonad + wetstorage + wetgut

which is lines 737-740 in DEB_euler
https://github.com/mrke/NicheMapR/blob/master/R/DEB_euler.R

Hope that helps.

All the best,
Mike

Hi Mike,

Thanks a lot. That worked perfectly! :)

Now I am simulating a frog and I am seeing some discrepancies between ectoR_devel and ectotherm too... with pct_wet = 100, the effect of evaporative cooling seems bigger with the ectoR_devel function compared to the ectotherm function (~3ºC in the warmest simulated day). Those differences disappear if I increase K_sub, which makes complete sense.

ectoR_devel also complains about Reynold's number being too low, but I guess that the same happens in the ectotherm function, with the only difference that the warning message is commented in CONV.f, right? And "only" warns about those low values not being available in Tracy 1976's Fig. 10, right?

Below I have pasted the code that I am using.

Thanks a lot in advance! All the best,
Urtzi

# run microclimate model in monthly mode at default site (Madison, Wisconsin, USA)
micro <- micro_global()

# extract full sun conditions
metout <- as.data.frame(micro$metout)
soil <- as.data.frame(micro$soil)

# get required inputs
TAs <- metout$TALOC
TGRDs <- soil$D0cm
TSKYs <- metout$TSKYC
VELs <- metout$VLOC
RHs <- metout$RHLOC
QSOLRs <- metout$SOLR
Zs <- metout$ZEN

K_subs <- micro$tcond[, 3]
# micro$tcond[, 3] <- 4; K_subs <- micro$tcond[, 3]

# use ectoR_devel to compute body temperature in open without respiratory heat loss

# or metabolic heat gain

TC <- unlist(lapply(1:length(TAs), function(x){ectoR_devel(
  Ww_g = 40, # wet weight, g

  shape = 4, # using frog geometry
  pct_wet = 100,

  alpha = 0.85, # solar absorptivity
  M_1 = 0, # turn of metabolic heat
  postur = 0, # average posture, half way between normal and parallel to sun
  pantmax = 0, # turn off respiratory heat exchange
  pct_cond = 40,

  K_sub = K_subs[x],
  #K_sub = 0.1,

  elev = micro$elev, # elevation from microclimate model

  Ww_g = 40, # wet weight, g

  shape = 4, # using frog geometry
  pct_wet = 100,

plot(time, TC, type = 'l', ylim = c(-25, 55), ylab = 'body temperature, deg C', xlab = 'month of year')
points(time, TC_ectotherm, type = 'l', col = 2)

Hi Urtzi,
That's an interesting issue you have exposed. The model is indeed being pushed a bit with 100% wet skin, so much conduction, and heavy solar radiation. The ectotherm model has some approaches for dealing with unstable situations that Warren Porter decided upon, e.g. changing to a different shape (from frog to sphere) that are not being done by the ectoR_devel. If you set the enberr parameter to 0.01 in the ectotherm model (this is the factor by which body mass is multiplied to get the tolerance for the energy balance solution), and cut the skin wetness to 80% (I've learned from discussions with Eric Riddell and computing resistance from skin wetness that this is a better upper value to use) then you'll get congruence between ectotherm and ectoR_devel. I'll explore this a bit more but in the meantime I've set the default energy balance (enberr) to 0.01 in the ectotherm model rather than the much lower value it had before.
All the best,
Mike

messages.subject: Output from multiple years
messages.body_plain:
Hey Mike! Got a more methods-y kind of question for you. Say I'm interested in looking at the NicheMapR output for a specific time period, and I pull multiple years to work with (for argument, let's say the years 1980-1983). I pull multiple years to account for extreme and rare climate events, so I'm more interested in average results from this time period rather than specific results for each year.

Here's the question: do I average the metout output for all years/days/hours before I run NicheMapR (resulting in a file representing a single "average" year with average climate conditions hour by hour), or should I run NicheMapR on each year separately and then average the output? Or does it not matter/or is this a really bad idea?

Best
Adam

messages.body_plain:
Hi Mike,
I had help from Urtzi, and we made a modified version of micro_global() called micro_glboal_drought() in the attached email with the goal of simulating drought by changing either changing 1) vapour pressure and 2) relative humidity (RH). Urtzi applied a "drought factor" (new function parameter 'dfact') to the vapour pressure and then converted it back to RH (lines 492-502). In the second version (micro_global_drought2), he directly applied the drought factor to RH (lines 1554-1558). And results are exactly the same (red and blue lines in plots below). Soooo, we are not entirely convinced that I did correctly the RH -> VP -> RH conversions... any insights to why this might be?

Note, drought factor 'dfact' with a value of 0.2 means 20% of the original RH or VP.

* Blue and red lines overlapped.

Cheers,
Niky

On Wed, 17 Aug 2022 at 22:35, NicheMapR <nich...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Hi Nicholas,
>
> Reducing the rainfall would seem to be the most obvious way to impose a drought though. It really depends on what process you're trying to modify for what species.
>
> Is it altering the water intake? That would then require a prediction of food water content and the possibility of drinking from rain. You could use the plantgro function to simulate plant water content as a function of soil water potential.
>
> Is it altering water loss? That would be driven by atmospheric water content, i.e. vapour pressure/humidity.
>
> To alter the vapour pressure, you'd need to modify the relative humidity coming from the global_climate.nc <http://global_climate.nc> file that is used as input. You'd have to convert it first to vapour pressure with the WETAIR function, drop it by the factor you're after, and then convert it back to relative humidity to then be passed to the microclimate model. That would require modifying the micro_global function.
>
> All the best,
> Mike
>
> On Wednesday, August 17, 2022 at 5:58:39 PM UTC+10 Nicholas wrote:
> > Hi everyone,
> > Is there a way to simulate drought with the micro_global function for a given location?
> >
> > There are many definitions of drought in the literature. For example, when there is a prolonged time with less than average precipitation, or an increase in vapor pressure deficit (VPD). I was thinking of changing the VPD given the non-standard lack of rainfall for a long period is a bit subjective. Some use time and others use below-average rainfall.

> > I had a look at the micro_global function on GitHub (https://github.com/mrke/NicheMapR/blob/master/R/micro_global.R) but there was no option for VPD. Any advice or recommendations that could help simulate drought?
